still_missing: The success criteria requires at least 2 studies comparing different antibiotic classes, but this material represents only one study. Additionally, while this study compares specific agents (Vancomycin vs. Metronidazole/Piperacillin-Tazobactam), it does not explicitly frame the comparison as 'Beta-lactams vs. Fluoroquinolones' as highlighted in the gap question, though Piperacillin-Tazobactam is a beta-lactam combination. It remains unclear if the neutral effect of Piperacillin-Tazobactam generalizes to other beta-lactams or if the negative effect of Vancomycin is consistent across other tumor types beyond melanoma.
usable_content: This study analyzed 876 patients with stage IV melanoma receiving ICI therapy to evaluate the impact of antibiotic type on outcomes. While overall antibiotic exposure showed no significant association with Time to Treatment Discontinuation (TTD) or Overall Survival (OS), specific antibiotic analysis revealed distinct differences: Vancomycin exposure was associated with decreased TTD (HR = 1.26) and worse OS (HR = 1.79), whereas exposure to Metronidazole and Piperacillin-Tazobactam had no significant impact on TTD or OS. This provides direct comparative evidence that negative impacts on ICI efficacy may be specific to certain antibiotic types rather than a class-wide effect. This study performed a class-specific analysis of antibiotic exposure (beta-lactams, carbapenems, vancomycin, anti-pseudomonas, anti-MRSA, anti-anaerobe) in 237 Hodgkin lymphoma patients receiving checkpoint inhibitor combinations prior to stem cell transplant. The authors reported that exposure to these specific antibiotic classes was not associated with inferior overall response rate, complete response, progression-free survival, or overall survival after adjustment for salvage line and regimen. This provides a concrete example of a study design that stratifies antibiotic exposure by class rather than treating all antibiotics as a single 'broad-spectrum' variable.
